title: Scientists discover breakthrough new way to find alien life
excerpt: Using AI and electrical signals, researchers could finally learn whether distant worlds are home to other living beings
content:
Scientists have discovered a breakthrough new method they hope will let them find life on other worlds.

Finding signs of life in space requires looking for "biosignatures", the marks left behind by living things. But actually spotting them can be difficult, given any equipment needs to be both sensitive enough to pick up any signals and compact enough to actually be sent to another planet.

Now, by combining artificial intelligence and electrical signals, researchers from the University of Osaka believe they have found a new method to find extraterrestrial life. And they hope that it could be powerful and small enough to be sent to other planets to find out whether we are alone in the universe.

Discovering living beings and separating them from nonliving chemicals and process is often done by looking at amino acids, the building blocks for proteins. Though amino acids have the same chemical formula, they come in two forms, the mirror image of each other – for living creatures, they are almost all L-forms, and sugars are D-forms, with nonliving processes producing each form in similar amounts.

Scientists believe that they could be able to use those different forms and their ratios as a biosignature that would indicate the existence of life. But actually doing so has been impractical: researchers have to get large groups of molecules, which is tough given the planets are so far away.

In an attempt to overcome that problem, researchers have been looking for ways of using electricity to detect those signals. That would be more simple, less sensitive to vibrations during the collection, get around the need to use chemicals.

Now researchers say they have made a breakthrough in that work.

In the new study, the scientists were able to measure molecules as they passed through a gap between two extremely thin pieces of gold wire. The waveforms of the current as it passes between those wires is different depending on which kind of amino acid is there, and so the equipment makes it possible to tell them apart by counting the molecules as they pass.

"By combining our nanogap tunneling technique with artificial intelligence, we were able to distinguish between the L- and D-forms of amino acids with over 80 per cent accuracy," said lead author, Takahito Oshiro. "This is the first discrimination of amino-acid chirality at the single-molecule level and constitutes a fundamental advance in chemical sensing."

To test the method, researchers used it on samples taken from Earth: one from the Murchison meteorite in Australia as well as soil from the Atacama Desert in Chile. It worked in a comparable way to traditional methods, allowing them to understand the composition of the amino acids involved.

Researchers hope they can use the technology to make small instruments that use electricity and are able to detect signs of alien life.

The work is reported in a new paper, 'Chiral discrimination of amino acids in meteorite and desert soil extracts via single-molecule nanogap conductance', published in the journal Nature Communications.
